m-cut: A re-anchor is a keep-0 rebase: the frame cache is cleared and the next frame is made like the first frame of a new video, from pure noise under the new prompt. Live it runs on a 2-step schedule (1000, 500). The decoder is restarted on that frame, because decoding it as a continuation gave a washed-out, ghosted chunk. Then the decoder dissolves from the last frame the viewer saw: frame k after the cut is (1 - a) times the old frame plus a times the new one, a = (k + 1) / (N + 1), N = 8, so the new scene is fully in after 0.5 s. Ishaan compared 12 scene-change variants; this one won: pop 67 to 79 for a clean hard cut, 10 to 11 with the 8-frame blend. The strip is from the live recording, frames 125 ms apart.
cover: Open with: nothing on these frames is a recording of a real scene. They are four moments from one continuous live run: a diffusion model drew every frame, and each change came from a spoken or typed sentence. The product is called Mirage (the lead's decision, 15 Nov 2026); the subtitle says what it is: live voice-steered video. Source of the frames: engine recording 20261115T003525Z-s003.mp4 on the live engine (frames at 0.5 s, 7 s, 30 s and 45 s; commands in between also added a red car and made it night).
clock: The live engine's /stats showed 191.5 ms generation and 21.9 ms decode per chunk on average at 16.0 fps. Generation and decode share the one GPU, so their sum is what counts against the 250 ms budget: about 36 ms to spare. Around commands generation rises to about 230 ms. At the model's native 480 x 832 generation alone took 417 ms per chunk on the L40S (MODEL_NOTES Gate 1 table), which is why the live size is 384 x 672.
hardware: The two L40S machines (AWS g6e.2xlarge) are madhacks-engine (live) and madhacks-engine-2 (tests). Spec numbers are from NVIDIA's datasheets: L40S 48 GB GDDR6, 864 GB/s; RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition 96 GB GDDR7, about 1.8 TB/s. Generation is a large matrix workload that also reads the 1.3B weights and the frame cache for every pass, so both bandwidth and compute matter. The only Blackwell number we quote is measured: about 150 ms per chunk at the full 832 x 480, on the demo machine on the night of 15 Nov 2026, against the 250 ms budget (the L40S measured 417 ms at that size). Every other number in the deck is from an L40S; say so if asked.
latency: Top part (before): the stage breakdown from 15 live commands at 00:55 UTC, before the latency deploy at 02:54 UTC. Bottom two cyan bars (after): only what was measured after the deploy, the median command-to-screen total (449 ms) and the cut chunk (162 ms in Ishaan's run, against 412 ms in the same run; the live stage median before was 345 ms). No per-stage breakdown after the deploy exists in the repo or on the board, so the other after-stages are not drawn. each bar is the median of that stage, so the bars only roughly add to the totals (server heard-to-shown 555 ms, page 596 ms). The voice bar is the page waiting for 200 ms of unchanged words; it applies to the mic only. The three amber stages are what we attacked: the cut chunk now runs on a 2-step schedule with the cache pass deferred (Ishaan measured 162 ms against 412 to 418 ms; defer_context and interrupt gave bit-identical frames to the reference, and the 2-step cut kept the same sharpness, 518 vs 519); interrupt stops the old-scene chunk being generated; flush drops old frames already queued. Result over the live harness runs, pinned sentences: median 717 to 449 ms, p90 737 to 498 ms (11 and 18 commands). A later harness at 04:30 UTC saw 299 to 362 ms. New sentences still wait about 2 s for Sonnet.
commands: The scene state is a base scene plus a list of named changes, each with a kind and a strength, plus a history for undo. Sonnet's operations are add, remove, set_strength, edit_base and new_scene, at most 6 per sentence; undo and reset are read by the dictionary so they never wait on the model. Strength words: "a little" is 0.3, "a lot more" is 1.3. Keyword table: 39 concept labels plus 242 aliases, 281 trigger words in all. Gate 3 (live, typed through the harness): all 14 steps understood and chips right; on screen, past about 5 objects the model drops some, so the demo keeps to about 4.
hard: This is the slide to slow down on. Every quarter of a second the model starts from random noise and must finish 4 new frames before the viewer needs them. Nothing is pre-rendered. The next four slides show four reasons this is hard: the clock, a model trained for something else, errors that compound, and open-ended language.
rejected: Every row was built and measured, then turned off for a stated reason. torch.compile: generation 193 to 148 ms median on machine 2, but frames are not equal to the uncompiled run (max pixel difference 255, sharpness up to 45% different), so it stays off; CUDA graphs crash on the model's cache code. Wan VAE: 157 ms vs 21.5 ms per chunk, nearly identical picture. 3 or 4 steps: slower and worse. 480 x 832: 417 ms generation alone. LongLive-style re-cache without a rebase: the world never changes and a 2.3 s stall. Keep-layout steer start (steer_anchor_t=800 with fixed noise): layout kept (tree moves 7 to 16 px instead of up to 194 px) but winter reaches only a white share of 0.10 to 0.12 on the meadow, against about 0.30 with the default; it is off live. Ishaan's 12-variant comparison picked the live method.
m-diffusion: The general form is x_t = alpha_t x_0 + sigma_t epsilon. Wan2.1 uses flow matching, where alpha_t = 1 - sigma_t, a straight line from the clean frame to noise. Causal Forcing++ was distilled so that 2 steps, at t = 1000 and t = 500, are enough for each new frame (4 steps on the very first frame of a video). The time grid is warped toward noise: the "500" step is at a noise level of about 0.83 (MODEL_NOTES, refresh noise section). A chunk is 3 passes: 2 denoising passes and one context pass that writes the clean frame into the frame cache. Measured on the L40S: 2 steps 218 ms, 3 steps 277 ms, 4 steps 349 ms per chunk; sharpness 783 / 721 / 688, and colour collapse came sooner with 4 steps.
demo: Demo cue. Meadow chain (all pinned, about 0.3 to 0.5 s each): make it winter, add a red car, make it night, add a lion, sunny, undo, make it a desert. Then hand the mic to a judge: a new sentence costs about 2 s because it goes to Claude Sonnet 5.5. Optional second chain: "new scene of a red sports car driving along a country road", then make it winter, make it a desert, make it night (neon city), make it autumn. Keep chains to about 4 objects at once: past about 5 the model drops some. Avoid "add a red car racing on a road" after the desert and "take me to the beach" on the car scene (known weak). If anything breaks: press Reset and say "that is live generation". The engine records every session as an mp4, which is the backup video.
pipeline: Walk the loop. 1: the page uses Chrome speech recognition; a spoken command is sent once the words have not changed for 200 ms. 2: a pinned sentence (133 of them) is answered in 4 to 9 ms; any other final sentence goes to one Claude Sonnet 5.5 call on Azure AI Foundry, about 1.4 s; on a timeout the keyword table and a MiniLM vector matcher answer instead. 3: the scene state applies the operations, keeps undo history and writes one prompt. 4: umT5-xxl turns the prompt into a 512 x 4096 tensor, cached by text. 5: the steering module and re-anchor policy decide when to cut. 6: Causal Forcing++ makes one latent frame per chunk in 2 denoising steps. 7: TAEHV decodes it to 4 frames in about 21 ms. 8: frames go to the browser as JPEG over a websocket through a Cloudflare quick tunnel.
language: All three happened to us on 14 Nov. "make it a desert" became a style pass-through, and the composed prompt was "a wide shot of a meadow with a single oak tree; the whole scene looks a desert", so the model kept the meadow and added flowers. "add a lion" was dropped because the keyword table did not know the word. The reversing car: the short base prompt drove backwards in 1 of 3 seeds; a 60 to 100 word prompt with direction cues went forward in 3 of 3. Long prompts of 60 to 100 words looked far better than comma-joined short ones (Ishaan's runs). That is why the Sonnet reader writes one full description of the scene for every new state.
added: The fair claim, from our own prior-art check: each piece is engineering on top of known methods; the combination is the new part. We found no other system with an undo stack and named, stackable operations on a live diffusion stream, but that is weaker than proof that none exists, so we do not say "first". Latency: 717 ms median before, 449 ms after, over the live harness runs, pinned sentences (board post 03:29 UTC). A new sentence takes about 2 s because of one Sonnet call.
limits: Say these before a judge finds them. Latency: pinned or cached sentences and undo about 0.45 to 0.5 s; new sentences 1.7 to 3.2 s measured, about 2 s typical, because of one Sonnet call. Layout: a command re-anchors from noise at full strength, so the shot is re-composed; the keep-layout option exists but winter then only partly arrives, so it is off. Gate 3: chips right after every step, but past about 5 objects the picture drops some. Gate 4c: early steering on partial speech is not shown. No real faces: the 1.3B model cannot draw a specific person. Resolution: 480 x 832 is 417 ms per chunk on the L40S. Pace words like "slowly" work since 03:52 UTC but are not in the demo.
compound: In words: the chance of a whole video is the product of the chance of each chunk given every chunk before it. The model only sees the last 21 latent frames (its attention window), and those frames are its own earlier output, so any error feeds back. Measured on the live engine before PR #83: over-saturated by 25 to 30 s and broken by 40 to 60 s. The fix (clean-anchor refresh with fixed noise) comes later in the deck.
fix-cut: A re-anchor makes a first-frame latent, which the video autoencoder normally decodes with a fresh state. The streaming decoder kept the last 3 latents of the old scene and decoded the new frame as a continuation, which gave a washed-out double image and a soft next chunk on every refresh and every command. Now the decoder restarts its stream state on every re-anchor while keeping the chunk count. Measured sharpness of the anchor chunk on a steer: meadow 110 before, 901 after; car 71 before, 361 after. A steer used to take about 3 ghosted chunks to reach the new scene; now it is one clean cut, which the 8-frame dissolve then softens.
team: Close by crediting the base work again. Then go back to the live video for questions. Likely questions: What did you build versus reuse? (Slides 2 and 3.) How fast is it? (Read the badge; pinned about 0.45 s, new sentence about 2 s.) What breaks it? (The limits slide.) Why an H100 for the demo? (480 x 832 is 417 ms per chunk on the L40S; we have no H100 measurements to quote.)
m-scale: Derivation. The Wan VAE compresses 8x in each spatial direction and 4x in time, with 16 latent channels: 384 x 672 becomes 48 x 84. The transformer cuts the latent into 2 x 2 patches: 24 x 42 = 1,008 tokens per latent frame. One latent frame is one chunk, 4 video frames, so there are 4 per second. The cache holds 21 latent frames, so attention can see up to 21,168 tokens. Compute estimate per pass: the usual 2 x parameters x tokens for the weight matrices, about 2.6 TFLOP, plus attention, 4 x layers x width x query tokens x key tokens, about 3.9 TFLOP. Three passes per chunk and four chunks per second give about 78 TFLOP per second of video. This is an estimate from the model shape, not a measurement; it ignores the text cross-attention and the decoder.
untrained: The model's attention window is 21 latent frames, about 5 seconds, and it was trained with one prompt per clip. We make it run without end and change the prompt while it plays. The four frames are all ours, from before the fixes: drift with no refresh (60 s after reset), the ghosted cut before the decoder restart (PR #83), "make it winter" before re-anchoring, where the model kept copying its old green frames and only added a white strip (Gate 2 first attempt), and a collapsed frame used as a known-bad frame for the vision judge. The reversing car: Ishaan measured the short base prompt driving backwards in 1 of 3 seeds; a long prompt with explicit direction words fixed it (3 of 3 forward).
next: Keep-layout: Ishaan's steer start options (steer_anchor_t=800 with fixed noise) keep the tree within 7 to 16 px instead of up to 194 px, but on the meadow winter reaches a white share of only 0.10 to 0.12 against about 0.30 with the defaults. Early steering: the partial reader already sends a provisional guess capped at 0.4, but a guess never re-anchors, so nothing shows. Sonnet skip: today only measured car worlds skip it. Resolution: 417 ms per chunk at 480 x 832 against 250 ms means at least 1.67 times faster generation. The four frames are one live car chain: start, make it winter, make it a desert, make it night.
fix-drift: Before PR #83 the live picture was over-saturated by 25 to 30 s and broken by 40 to 60 s. A refresh from the last frame bakes the damage in, so the backend saves a clean anchor 3 chunks after each reset or scene change and refreshes from it. The first version still re-rolled the scene each time, because each refresh drew fresh noise at the warped step (sigma about 0.83). Seeding that noise from the video seed and the anchor's chunk number made every refresh return to the same picture: re-roll 30.4 down to 10.9, the same as normal motion over 1 s (12.1), with no drift over 360 chunks. Both measured by Ishaan on the L40S.
testing: Two layers. Layer A runs every sentence in acceptance/sentences.json through the live reader stack and checks the chips and prompt words. Layer B plays the cases on the real engine, takes the frame 3 s after each step and asks a Claude Sonnet 5.5 vision call yes/no questions plus a picture-quality question. Calibration: 16 frames with known contents, 4 of them known-bad, 47 questions: 47 of 47 right, but in-sample, because the first wording of the quality question failed 2 good frames (45 of 47) and was reworded on the same frames. Live run 1: 20 of 23 steps pass; run 2 at 03:42: 19 of 23. The failures are real picture faults (the car on the water for "take me to the beach", no road for "add a red car racing on a road"), and we checked each by eye. Default suite: 969 passed on devbox at 04:54 UTC.
m-steer: The steerer is the credited idea, implemented by Ishaan: per-token spherical interpolation of direction with a linear blend of length, falling back to a plain linear blend for zero or parallel vectors, and a min-jerk easing curve r cubed times (10 - 15r + 6r squared). Each new move starts from wherever the conditioning is now, so commands can interrupt each other. Strength uses the same blend between the prompt without the change and the prompt with it; s above 1 extrapolates, capped at 1.3. Dashed line on the chart: a plain linear ramp for comparison. The honest part: on this model the blend alone is not enough, because the frame cache keeps pulling the picture back to the old scene, so commands send a 1-chunk ramp and the re-anchor policy fires a cut once the ramp reaches the target.
overnight: Four of us directed AI coding agents, and every change was tested, reviewed and measured before it reached the demo. Counts taken at 17:55 UTC on 15 Nov: 185 merged pull requests (gh pr list --state merged), 617 commits on main (git log origin/main), 846 test functions (def test_ in */tests/*.py). 84 of the 185 merged pull requests also have a review or comment from the Greptile code-review bot; its findings were fixed in follow-up commits. There is no CI server: by team rule the author's agent ran the test suite before each merge. Two NVIDIA L40S machines ran side by side all night. One ran the live engine, and we tested it by hand, speaking commands at the real stream. The other was a test bench: agents measured each change there first, with frame sheets, fixed seeds and a vision judge that grades frames from the live video (47 of 47 right on frames with known contents). Only measured changes went to the live engine. Before the final redesign went live, a regression sweep replayed 879 steps of saved command chains through the old and the new code and compared them; the regressions it found were fixed first (issue #285). Measured and then rejected (slide 20): torch.compile, 3 and 4 denoising steps, the full Wan decoder and the keep-layout steering setting. Later a Blackwell test machine ran the full 832 x 480 size (next slide). Update the counts right before presenting; they will have grown.
